newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: FOCUS-EU to take U.S. to WTO over Helms-Burton.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU to take U.S. to WTO over Helms-Burton.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers sprung a surpise on Tuesday by deciding not to wait to file a complaint with the World Trade Organisation against Washington's anti-Cuba laws.
The foreign ministers ended months of uncertainty when they agreed to challenge the United States on its controversial Helms-Burton Act at the WTO in Geneva.

Diplomatic sources said the decision even caught EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan by surprise. Brittan had been expecting the decision to be deferred until after U.S presidential elections on November 5, the sources said.
Although the WTO panel will convene after the election, the EU's complaint will formally be lodged on October 16, EU officials said.
"The view is that this is something that can't wait," an Irish EU presidency spokesman said. "EU interests need to be protected and prevaricating on it would only send a weak and indecisive signal."
While he may have been surprised, Brittan was clearly delighted with the decision. "We have shown the world that the EU has the capacity and political will to defend its interests," he told Reuters.
The Helms-Burton Act, an amalgamation of years of anti-Cuba legislation, was passed in July to a chorus of indignant opposition from some of Washington's strongest trade partners.

Among other things, it allows naturalised Americans to sue in U.S. courts foreign companies or individuals deemed to have gained from investments in Cuban property confiscated since the communist revolution of 1959.

The EU has been considering a raft of retaliatory measures to the act and also to the D'Amato Bill -- which seeks to outlaw trade with Iran and Libya -- and escalating a WTO dispute was considered a drastic, albeit dramatic last resort.
Analysts have suggested in the past that the EU was wary of escalating the WTO dispute in case the U.S. employed a rarely-used "national security interests" clause in its defence.
But Brittan said fear of this "was not an issue" when the foreign ministers came to their decision. "What is the use of creating a dispute settlements process if you are afraid of using it," he said.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said that the question of whether or not the issue went to the WTO before the U.S. elections was largely irrelevant.
"I don't think that the question of elections in the United States...should determine European Union policy," he said.
In July, foreign ministers gave Brittan a mandate to examine four retaliatory measures -- including the WTO dispute.

The first -- creating a watch list of U.S. companies involved in litigation involving EU companies has already been approved but a second -- allowing European companies to counter-sue U.S. litigants -- has been sent back to the Commission for "fine tuning", Brittan said.
He expected it to be passed later this month at the next foreign ministers' meeting.
A fourth proposal, to slap visa restrictions on Americans involved in Helms-Burton lawsuits, was "a lot trickier", Brittan said and needed more study.
